opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've ridden in Waymo quite a few times now, in San Francisco and also in Phoenix, and honestly the first ride is the most memorable. You get in, there's nobody in the driver's seat, the steering wheel turns by itself, and for the first two or three minutes you're a bit nervous, watching every intersection. Then after about ten minutes you forget about it. You start checking your phone, you're just a passenger. That shift, from anxiety to boredom, tells you a lot. When the technology becomes boring, it's mature.

What impressed me most wasn't the easy stretches. It was the long-tail situations: a double-parked delivery truck, a pedestrian who hesitates in the crosswalk, a cyclist cutting in, construction cones that weren't there yesterday. The car handled them smoothly and, frankly, more cautiously and politely than many human drivers. It doesn't get distracted, doesn't get tired, doesn't drink.

So my view is that, technically, L4 autonomous driving in defined areas has crossed the threshold. It's no longer a question of *whether* it works; it's a question of scale, cost, and regulation. Waymo has accumulated an enormous number of fully driverless miles, and the safety data, measured against human drivers on injury crashes, is quite convincing.

That said, there are still challenges. The cost of the vehicle and the sensor suite needs to come down further. Expanding to new cities still takes a lot of mapping, validation, and work with local governments. Extreme weather like heavy snow is harder. And there's the social side: public trust, insurance, liability, how first responders interact with these cars.

But I'd say we're at an inflection point. In China we're seeing the same thing with Apollo Go in Wuhan and other cities, operating at very large scale. When I was at Baidu, we used to say autonomous driving would follow a "long tail, then sudden acceleration" curve. For years progress looked slow, and people said it was always five years away. Now I think we're in the acceleration phase. Within the next several years, robotaxis will be a normal part of life in many major cities, and that's going to be the first truly large-scale deployment of physical AI, AI that actually operates in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
I rode Waymo quite a few times in San Francisco and Phoenix, and honestly, the first thing it tells me is that we've crossed a threshold. Five or six years ago, when I was still at Baidu working on Apollo, we had the same ambition, but the feeling in the car was different. You were always a little tense. Now you get in a Waymo, there's no one in the driver's seat, and within two or three minutes you forget about it. You check your phone, you take a call. That psychological shift, going from "watching the car" to "trusting the car," is the real signal of maturity.

Technically, what impresses me is the smoothness in complex urban scenarios. San Francisco is not an easy city. Steep hills, double-parked cars, cyclists cutting in, pedestrians who don't look. Waymo handles unprotected left turns, construction zones, people stepping off the curb, and it does it conservatively but not stupidly. A few years ago, systems would freeze or brake too hard in those situations. Now the behavior feels like a careful, experienced driver.

But I want to be careful not to overstate it. Mature in a geofenced area with high-definition maps and heavy remote support is not the same as mature everywhere. Waymo is running tens of thousands of rides a week, maybe more, and that's wonderful, but it's in a handful of cities, with good weather, with years of data collected on those exact streets. The last part of the problem, the long tail of rare events, is still very expensive to solve. And the unit economics are not yet proven. Each vehicle still carries a lot of sensors, a lot of compute, and there's an operations team behind it.

So my conclusion is this. The question "can it work?" has been answered. Yes, L4 robotaxis work. The remaining questions are "how fast can it scale," "how cheap can it become," and "how does it generalize to new cities." That's an engineering and business problem now, not a science problem. And I think China will move quite fast on this, because the cost structure of the vehicles and the density of the cities both favor rapid deployment. Baidu's Apollo Go in Wuhan is already showing that. In the next three to five years, I expect this to go from a novelty to something people in major cities just use without thinking about it.

astra-6.text: My experience riding in Waymo gave me the sense that autonomous driving has moved beyond a research demonstration. In a defined operating area, it can provide a practical service, and that’s a significant milestone. But I would distinguish that from being able to drive anywhere, under any conditions. One ride can give you a feel for how the system behaves; it cannot establish its overall safety. So I’m optimistic, but maturity has to be measured by consistent performance across many trips and difficult situations, not just a smooth individual ride.

sol-6.1.text:
My experience riding in Waymo gave me the sense that autonomous driving has moved beyond a research demonstration. Within the areas where it operates, it can provide a useful service, and the ride can feel quite ordinary—which is a meaningful achievement.

But we should distinguish that from a car that can drive anywhere, in any weather, under any conditions. Handling unusual situations reliably is still the hard part. So I would say the technology is mature enough for commercial deployment within defined operating conditions, while broader autonomy remains a work in progress.
